# Introduction

Trusting science at large requires rigor and reproducibility, hence clear communication of experiments has become one of the cornerstones of good scientific practices. To this end, many scientific projects rely on detailed description of experimental design and protocols in manuscripts, visual diagrams, standard reporting guidelines and checklists, and more-or-less standard software, all to provide enough details to reproduce the findings.

Trust in code and data is also becoming more and more critical today, as we increasingly rely on AI and machines to facilitate scientific research. The need for reproducibility of scientific experiments has become essential for building trust in automated processes, especially at scale.

The context of this paper is how scientific workflows and everything related to that (study protocols, experimental designs, data, etc) can be communicated for rigor and reproducibility in modern days.


## Problem statement

As with everything else, trust and understanding requires a complete description of systems. And a complete description of a computing system requires both 1) a data model and 2) a process model [@sehgal2011]. The data model describes the structure and semantics of the data, while the process model describes the workflow of generating and making sense of the data. The cognitive science industry is no exception to this requirement. Yet, most efforts are focused on standardized data (which is good in isolation), while formalizing the processes that generate the data are often neglected. Consequently, the common practice for process models rely on reusing common software and codes (see for example, REF, REF, REF), and more recently language models that encapsulate the implicit knowledge of experimental designs (REF).

 The lack of rigor process models is particularly problematic in cognitive science, probably because the complexity of the experiments and the multidisciplinary diversity of the stakeholders make it difficult to communicate and effectively share the experiments and findings with everyone.


## Current approach and its limitations

Current strategies to define and communicate experimental workflows are either informal as plain textual descriptions in manuscripts accompanied by codes and figures in arbitrary formats. Some of the strategies researchers use to compensate for the lack of clarity in natural language or diversity of codes are as follows:

**Box and arrow figures** explains the workflow and the data in a more abstract way. These are limited because of the medium, or task-specific formats. There are efforts like UML in software engineering, or CONSORT in experimental sciences, but they are limited an inefficient to capture the complexity of modern data and softwares (e.g., MLOps). Given the fact that several stakeholders in scientific research each requires different kinds of communication, those diagramming are required to be separately tailored for each stakeholder; making it impossible to share via common scientific communication outlets such as manuscripts. At the end they are just arbitrary description of what actually happened during the scientific experiment, neither the texts nor the visual diagrams are executable for engineers to re-use.
- **Checklists**, and pre-defined forms (e.g., pre-registration) address the need for structured text descriptions but they do not directly addresses the need for exploration required by rigorous science (e.g., by keeping track of changes or promoting version control). Keeping history is difficult because of the inherent unstructured-ness of natural language descriptions, and the way they are stored: formatted texts in proprietary PDF, DOCX, and on data silos that will never change.
- **Schemas, standards, ontologies, and custom packages** make decisions and designs machine-readable, but they do not capture the two different aspects of the modern science: domain-specific (as in asking the right question) and technical (as in using the right software architecture). They are either tailored for domain experts (e.g., NiBabel), or technical experts (e.g., UML). The technical solutions are also often specific to particular use cases, e.g., MLOps or GitHub actions, and do not address the need for several levels of expertise that a scientific project requires, from funding agencies and public audiences, to software engineers and non-expert assistants who develop the tools, collect the data, and manage the process. Recent efforts in cognitive science have mainly focused on data models, such as BIDS [@gorgolewski2016bids] and Psych-DS [@REF], which provide a structured way to describe the data collected during experiments. However, data models do not address the need for an end-to-end description of the workflows that generate, analyze, and report the data. Recent paradigm shifts in how data is managed (@REF) and how software is implemented (e.g., @REF) requires more flexible and adaptable workflows that can handle multi-modal data and changing environments. 
- **Codes** (source code, scripts, MLOps packages, CI jobs, etc) make pipeline definitions clear, but requires a lot of effort to be readable and shareable which is a luxury for scientists whose main task is address research questions. They also often include terminologies and require environments which are not tailored for other non-expert stakeholders they like to communicate with. Sharing those codes is also a limiting factor, as it requires intellectual property management or open sourcing the project which is not always feasible for human-involved scientific projects.


However, these formats are not always easy to share or execute, specifically given the multitude of expertise required for experimental sciences (as in scientists, data collectors, analysts, funding agencies, etc). The situation is even worse when the methods are described in a language that is not the native language of the reader or a programming language that is proprietary or outdated. Interpreting those texts and supporting diagrams also require specialized knowledge that is not always available to all the stakeholders, making them inaccessible to non-experts and hindering the reproducibility of the experiments. We can however leverage practices in safety-critical disciplines that require trust (e.g., finance or healthcare) and apply them to experimental cognitive sciences.

## Our contributions

To address this, our contribution is two-fold:
A formal language to describe processes in scientific studies that can be interpreted and executed by both humans (at different levels of expertise) and machines (for different purposes).
A proof-of-concept interface to model and run the experiments without the need for specialized knowledge.

To this end we propose Studyflow, a formal language to describe cognitive experiments, and Studyflow Modeler, a tool to design and test cognitive experiments using the Studyflow language.

Studyflow is based on BPMN [Business Process Model and Notation; @white2004introduction], a standard for process modeling that is widely used in the industry. Just like its counterparts to model data, BPMN is a graphical language to formally describe workflows, making them easy to understand (by human) and execute (by machine). Studyflow extends BPMN with additional elements to describe scientific experiments, such as elements for data collection, data transformation, modeling, checklists, and other patterns common in an experimental study.

Additionally, Studyflow Modeler is a web-based tool that demonstrates how to design, test, and run cognitive experiments using the Studyflow language. It provides a graphical interface to create and edit Studyflow diagrams, as well as a simulator to run the workflow before deployment. The tool is designed to be easy to use, even for domain experts with no specialized technical experience.


## Benefits
In section X, several use cases of applying studyflow for common patterns in research will be presented to demonstrate the benefits of using studyflows in practice. But generally, using studyflow for scientific research workflows will benefit experimental research because:

Data models are not sufficient to reproduce the experiments. Full reproducibility requires an explicit process model to accompany the data model. Studyflow provides domain-specific elements for 1) activities including cognitive tests, questionnaires, instructions, and 2) data including specialized datasets that align with best practices like BDM (Behaverse Data Model), BIDS, Psych-DS, and Kedro to name a few.
Help all stakeholders understand complex research protocols using easily readable diagrams.
Provide a natural basis for collaboration between researchers, ethics committees, data scientists, software engineers, and other stakeholders through a coherent visual representation.
Reduce the effort and risk of experimental design through graphical decomposition of research workflows into well-defined activities, events, and gateways, and simulation of the workflow before deployment.
Allow study protocols to be defined simply and unambiguously using a formal machine-readable format that supports version control.
Simplify reproducibility of studies using specifications that can be automatically validated, shared, and executed.
Support the FAIR principles by making processes such as experimental protocols findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable.
Enable the development of a library of reusable research components across cognitive tests, questionnaires, instructions, and data processing pipelines.
